theme: “For such a time as this”; the king’s banquet; Haman exposed
readingInstruction: Read Esther 4:1-7:10. Esther is called to risk her life for her people. Read for the turning point in 4:14, and for the reversal at the end of chapter 7.
settingTheScene: When Mordecai learns of the decree, he puts on sackcloth and ashes and weeps in the city. Esther, in the palace, hears of it. Anyone who approaches the king unsummoned may be put to death, unless the king holds out the golden scepter. Esther has not been called in thirty days. Mordecai’s message to her is one of the great speeches of the Bible.
observation: “And in every province… there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting” (4:3).
“For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish” (4:14).
“And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (4:14).
“Go, gather all the Jews to be found in Susa, and hold a fast on my behalf” (4:16).
“On that night the king could not sleep. And he gave orders to bring the book of memorable deeds” (6:1).
“What honor or dignity has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?” (6:3).
“So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (7:10).
interpretation:
Mordecai’s message is the heart of the book. He makes two points. First, Esther cannot hide in the palace: “Do not think to yourself that in the king’s palace you will escape.” Second, God’s purpose does not depend on her. “Relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place.” This is as close as the book comes to naming God. Then comes the question: “Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” It is a call to see one’s position as a calling.

Esther’s response grows from fear to courage. She asks for a three-day fast, which means prayer in all but name, and says, “If I perish, I perish.” She will go to the king, trusting not in her beauty but in God. When she enters, the king holds out the scepter. She does not blurt out her request. She invites the king and Haman to a banquet, then to a second one. This is not hesitation but wisdom.

Meanwhile, the narrative shifts to a sleepless night. The king “could not sleep,” and so he calls for the chronicles. They open to the record of Mordecai’s good deed. The ironies multiply. Haman, who has just come to ask permission to hang Mordecai, is asked what should be done for the man the king delights to honor. Thinking it is himself, he proposes royal robes and a parade, and then must lead Mordecai through the streets.

At the second banquet, Esther names her request: “Let my life be granted me, and my people.” Haman is exposed, and the gallows he built for Mordecai becomes his own. “Sleeplessness” in the ordinary world is a vehicle for providence.
connection: Moses faced the same choice in Hebrews 11:24-26, giving up Pharaoh’s palace to be mistreated with the people of God. Jesus said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Psalm 7:15-16 and Proverbs 26:27 describe the trap that falls on the one who set it. Acts 17:26 says God determined the allotted periods of nations. 1 Peter 4:10: use your gifts to serve others.
application:
Ask: for what “such a time as this” might God have put you where you are?

Fast and pray before a major decision, as Esther and the Jews did.

Notice the people God has placed in your path, and be ready to speak up for them.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to show you what purpose he has put you where you are.
Ask for courage to speak when it costs you.
Ask for wisdom in choosing the right moment.
